docs.title: graphemes++
docs.text:
A Python library for accurate grapheme-level segmentation and processing, designed specifically for Indic scripts like Tamil and Sinhala.

Standard string processing libraries operate on Unicode code points. However, Indic scripts use complex sequences of code points such as consonant-vowel combinations and zero-width joiners to render a single visual grapheme. graphemes++ parses these visual clusters accurately.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Accurate Segmentation: Resolves multi-byte visual clusters and conjuncts effectively.
  • Language Aware: Contains specialized logic for Tamil (e.g., க்ஷ, ஸ்ரீ) and Sinhala (ZWJ sequences).
  • Phonetic Transliteration: Decompose graphemes into phonetic bases and vowels, and compose them back.
  • Robust Metrics: Includes GraphemeCHRF and Character Error Rate (CER) scaled properly to grapheme boundaries rather than code points, leading to more accurate NLP evaluation.
  • Distance Algorithms: Computes true grapheme-aware Levenshtein and Hamming distances.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from graphemes_plusplus import Graphemizer

text = "ஸ்ரீ மதி"
g = Graphemizer(text)

print(g.graphemes)
# Output: ['ஸ்ரீ', ' ', 'ம', 'தி']

print(len(g))
# Output: 4

docs.title: Composer
docs.text: The Composer class handles grapheme composition for Sinhala and Tamil text. It enables the recomposition of standard grapheme clusters from decomposed phonetic sequences.

docs.title: Class Definition
docs.text:
class Composer

Module: graphemes_plusplus.decomposer

All methods are @classmethod - no instantiation required.

docs.title: compose(text: str) → str
docs.text:
Composes a decomposed sequence back into standard grapheme clusters.

compose(text: str) → str
Parameter Type Description text str Decomposed phonetic sequence Returns str Recomposed standard text 
>>> from graphemes_plusplus import compose
>>> compose("க்ஆ")
'கா'

docs.title: Tamil
docs.text:
A sequence of a mei (consonant base + pulli) and an uyir (vowel) is merged back into a single grapheme:

Mei Uyir → Output க் அ → க க் ஆ → கா க் இ → கி க் உ → கு

docs.title: Sinhala
docs.text:
Sinhala consonant bases and vowels are similarly merged:

Base Vowel → Output ක් අ → ක ක් ආ → කා ක් ඇ → කැ

docs.title: Language Detection
docs.text:
The Composer automatically detects the script using Unicode ranges:

Script Unicode Range Tamil U+0B80 – U+0BFF Sinhala U+0D80 – U+0DFF

Mixed scripts Non-Tamil and non-Sinhala characters (English, punctuation, numbers) pass through unchanged during composition.

docs.title: Tamil Constants
docs.text:
• TAMIL_VOWELS - 12 Tamil vowels (உயிர் எழுத்துக்கள்): அ, ஆ, இ, ஈ, உ, ஊ, எ, ஏ, ஐ, ஒ, ஓ, ஔ
  • TAMIL_ACCENT_SYMBOLS - 12 Tamil vowel diacritics: (empty), ா, ி, ீ, ு, ூ, ெ, ே, ை, ொ, ோ, ௌ

docs.title: Sinhala Constants
docs.text:
• SINHALA_VOWELS - 18 Sinhala vowels: අ, ආ, ඇ, ඈ, ඉ, ඊ, උ, ඌ, ...
  • SINHALA_ACCENT_SYMBOLS - 18 Sinhala vowel diacritics
  • ZWJ_CHARS - Zero Width Joiner character combinations specific to Sinhala

docs.text:

docs.title: Decomposer
docs.text: The Decomposer class handles grapheme decomposition for Sinhala and Tamil text. It encapsulates language-specific phonetic rules, enabling character-level transformations needed for NLP tokenization and metric evaluation.

docs.title: Class Definition
docs.text:
class Decomposer

Module: graphemes_plusplus.decomposer

All methods are @classmethod - no instantiation required.

docs.title: decompose(text: str) → str
docs.text:
Decomposes Tamil and Sinhala strings into fundamental phonetic sequences. Punctuation and spaces are unaffected.

decompose(text: str) → str
Parameter Type Description text str Input text containing Tamil or Sinhala characters Returns str Decomposed phonetic sequence 
>>> from graphemes_plusplus import decompose
>>> decompose("கா")
'க்ஆ'  # consonant base + vowel

docs.title: Tamil
docs.text:
Each Tamil grapheme is split into a mei (consonant base + pulli) and an uyir (vowel):

Input → Mei Uyir க → க் அ கா → க் ஆ கி → க் இ கு → க் உ

docs.title: Sinhala
docs.text:
Sinhala graphemes follow a similar pattern with consonant base + hal + vowel:

Input → Base Vowel ක → ක් අ කා → ක් ආ කැ → ක් ඇ

docs.text:

Script Unicode Range Tamil U+0B80 – U+0BFF Sinhala U+0D80 – U+0DFF

Mixed scripts Non-Tamil and non-Sinhala characters (English, punctuation, numbers) pass through unchanged during decomposition.

docs.title: Distance Functions
docs.text:
Grapheme-aware string distance functions that correctly measure edit distances over visual character units rather than raw Unicode code points.

Module: graphemes_plusplus.distance

docs.title: levenshtein(s1: str, s2: str) → int
docs.text:
Computes the grapheme-aware Levenshtein distance (minimum edit distance) between two strings.

levenshtein(s1: str, s2: str) → int
Parameter Type Description s1 str First input string s2 str Second input string Returns int Minimum number of grapheme-level insertions, deletions, and substitutions 
>>> from graphemes_plusplus import levenshtein
>>> levenshtein("ஸ்ரீ", "ஸ்ரி")
1
>>> levenshtein("ක්‍රම", "කම")
1

Why grapheme-aware? Standard Levenshtein on raw Unicode would count ஸ்ரீ → ஸ்ரி as multiple edits because the underlying code points differ in count. Grapheme-aware Levenshtein correctly identifies this as a single grapheme substitution.

docs.title: hamming(s1: str, s2: str) → int
docs.text:
Computes the grapheme-aware Hamming distance between two strings. Both strings must have the same number of graphemes.

hamming(s1: str, s2: str) → int
Parameter Type Description s1 str First input string s2" |str` Second input string (must have equal grapheme count) Returns int Number of positions where graphemes differ 
>>> from graphemes_plusplus import hamming
>>> hamming("ஸ்ரீ", "ஸ்ரீ")
0

Equal length required The Hamming distance is only defined for strings with equal numbers of graphemes. If the grapheme counts differ, textdistance will handle the mismatch according to its own convention.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Both functions internally:

  1. Create Graphemizer instances for each input string
  2. Convert to list[str] of grapheme clusters
  3. Pass these lists to textdistance algorithms
graph LR
    A["Input Strings"] --> B["Graphemizer(s1)"]
    A --> C["Graphemizer(s2)"]
    B --> D["list[str]"]
    C --> E["list[str]"]
    D --> F["textdistance algorithm"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Distance (int)"]

    style A fill:#7c4dff,color:#fff
    style G fill:#00bfa5,color:#fff

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Graphemizer - Creates the grapheme lists used for comparison
  • Metrics - Higher-level evaluation metrics built on distance functions

docs.title: Graphemizer
docs.text: The Graphemizer class is the core entry point of graphemes++. It takes raw text, applies normalization, and segments it into linguistically correct grapheme clusters.

docs.title: Class Definition
docs.text:
class Graphemizer(string: str)

Module: graphemes_plusplus.graphemizer

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description string str The input text to segment into graphemes

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Type Description graphemes list[str] The list of segmented grapheme clusters raw_string str The original input string (before normalization)

docs.title: __len__() → int
docs.text:
Returns the number of grapheme clusters.

>>> g = Graphemizer("ஸ்ரீ மதி")
>>> len(g)
4

docs.title: __iter__()
docs.text:
Makes the Graphemizer instance iterable over its grapheme clusters.

>>> g = Graphemizer("ஸ்ரீ மதி")
>>> for grapheme in g:
...     print(grapheme)
ஸ்ரீ

ம
தி

docs.title: Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
The Graphemizer follows a two-stage pipeline:

graph LR
    A[Raw Text] --> B[Normalizer]
    B --> C[GraphemeSplitter]
    C --> D[List of Graphemes]

    style A fill:#7c4dff,color:#fff
    style D fill:#00bfa5,color:#fff
  1. Normalize - Unicode NFC normalization + Tamil/Sinhala-specific character fixups
  2. Split - Extended grapheme clustering that handles conjuncts and ZWJ sequences

docs.title: Tamil Segmentation
docs.text:
>>> g = Graphemizer("கொண்டுவந்து")
>>> g.graphemes
['கொ', 'ண்', 'டு', 'வ', 'ந்', 'து']

docs.title: Sinhala Segmentation
docs.text:
>>> g = Graphemizer("ක්‍රිකට්")
>>> g.graphemes
['ක්‍රි', 'ක', 'ට්']

docs.title: Mixed Script
docs.text:
>>> g = Graphemizer("Hello வணக்கம்!")
>>> g.graphemes
['H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o', ' ', 'வ', 'ண', 'க்', 'க', 'ம்', '!']

Normalization is automatic The Graphemizer automatically normalizes input text before segmentation. You don't need to pre-process your text unless you want explicit control over the normalization step.

docs.text:

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Grapheme-aware evaluation metrics for NLP tasks involving Tamil and Sinhala text. Includes GraphemeCHRF (chrF/chrF++) and CER (Character Error Rate).

Module: graphemes_plusplus.metric

docs.title: GraphemeCHRF
docs.text:
Computes the chrF(++) metric at the grapheme level. Extends SacreBLEU's CHRF class to operate on grapheme clusters instead of raw Unicode characters.

class GraphemeCHRF(char_order=6, word_order=0, beta=2, ...)

Inherits from: sacrebleu.metrics.chrf.CHRF

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Inherits all parameters from SacreBLEU's CHRF. Key parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description char_order int 6 Maximum order of character (grapheme) n-grams word_order int 0 Maximum order of word n-grams. Set to 2 for chrF++ beta float 2 Balance between precision and recall lowercase bool False Whether to lowercase before comparison whitespace bool" |False` Whether to include whitespace graphemes in n-grams

docs.title: Configurations
docs.text:
chrF (default)

from graphemes_plusplus.metric import GraphemeCHRF

chrf = GraphemeCHRF()  # word_order=0

chrF++

from graphemes_plusplus.metric import GraphemeCHRF

chrf_pp = GraphemeCHRF(word_order=2)  # includes word n-grams

docs.title: corpus_score(hypotheses, references) → CHRFScore
docs.text:
Compute corpus-level chrF score.

>>> chrf = GraphemeCHRF()
>>> score = chrf.corpus_score(
...     ["வணக்கம் உலகம்"],      # hypotheses
...     [["வணக்கம் உலகம்"]]     # references (list of lists)
... )
>>> print(score.score)
100.0

docs.title: sentence_score(hypothesis, references) → CHRFScore
docs.text:
Compute sentence-level chrF score.

>>> chrf = GraphemeCHRF()
>>> score = chrf.sentence_score("සිංහල", ["සිංහල"])
>>> print(score.score)
100.0

docs.title: How It Differs from Standard chrF
docs.text: Aspect Standard chrF GraphemeCHRF Unit Unicode code points Grapheme clusters ஸ்ரீ treated as 4 separate characters 1 grapheme Sinhala ZWJ Broken into parts Kept as single grapheme Better for Latin scripts Indic scripts (Tamil, Sinhala)

docs.title: CER
docs.text:
Computes the Character Error Rate between a hypothesis and reference string at the grapheme level.

CER(hypothesis: str, reference: str) → float

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description hypothesis str The predicted/generated string reference str The ground truth string Returns float CER value (0.0 = perfect match)

docs.title: Formula
docs.text: \[ \text{CER} = \frac{\text{LevenshteinDistance}(\text{hyp}, \text{ref})}{\text{len}(\text{ref\_graphemes})} \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
>>> from graphemes_plusplus.metric import CER
>>> CER("வணக்கம்", "வணக்கம்")
0.0
>>> CER("", "வணக்கம்")
1.0

Edge cases - If both hypothesis and reference are empty, CER returns 0.0 - If only the reference is empty but hypothesis is not, CER returns 1.0

docs.title: Character N-gram F-score
docs.text:
Computes the F-score between a hypothesis and reference string based on grapheme-level n-gram overlap.

character_ngram_fscore(hypothesis: str, reference: str, n: int = 2) → float

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description hypothesis str The predicted/generated string reference str The ground truth string n int Size of the character n-gram (default: 2 for bigrams) Returns float F-score value (between 0.0 and 1.0)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
>>> from graphemes_plusplus.metric import character_ngram_fscore
>>> character_ngram_fscore("ප්‍රධාන", "ප්‍රධාන")
1.0
>>> character_ngram_fscore("අධ්‍යාපනික", "අධ්‍යාපනික", n=3)
1.0

docs.title: BPC (Bits-per-Character)
docs.text:
Approximates the Bits-per-Character (BPC) metric at the grapheme level. Matching graphemes are assigned a high probability (0.9) and mismatches a low probability (0.1).

BPC(hypothesis: str, reference: str) → float

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description hypothesis str The predicted/generated string reference str The ground truth string Returns float The approximated BPC value (lower is better)

docs.title: Formula
docs.text: \[ \text{BPC} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log_2(P(c_i)) \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
>>> from graphemes_plusplus.metric import BPC
>>> BPC("දැනුම", "දැනුම")
0.1520030934
>>> BPC("දැනුම", "විද්‍යා")
3.3219280949

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Distance Functions - The Levenshtein function used by CER
  • Graphemizer - Segments text into graphemes before metric computation

docs.title: Install from Source
docs.text:
Currently, graphemes++ is installed from source via Git clone:

Using uv (recommended)

git clone https://github.com/vmenan/graphemes_plusplus.git
cd graphemes_plusplus
uv sync

Using pip

git clone https://github.com/vmenan/graphemes_plusplus.git
cd graphemes_plusplus
pip install -e .

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
graphemes++ depends on the following packages (installed automatically):

Package Version Purpose grapheme ≥ 0.6.0 Base Unicode grapheme clustering textdistance ≥ 4.6.3 Levenshtein & Hamming distance algorithms sacrebleu ≥ 2.0.0 chrF/chrF++ metric base class

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
After installation, verify everything works:

>>> from graphemes_plusplus import Graphemizer
>>> g = Graphemizer("வணக்கம்")
>>> g.graphemes
['வ', 'ண', 'க்', 'க', 'ம்']

Ready to go! If you see the grapheme list output without errors, the installation is complete. Head to the Quick Start guide next.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide walks you through the core features of graphemes++ in under 5 minutes.

docs.title: 1. Segment Text into Graphemes
docs.text:
The Graphemizer class is the primary entry point. It takes a string, normalizes it, and splits it into proper grapheme clusters.

from graphemes_plusplus import Graphemizer

# Tamil text
g = Graphemizer("ஸ்ரீ மதி")
print(g.graphemes)  # ['ஸ்ரீ', ' ', 'ம', 'தி']
print(len(g))       # 4

The Graphemizer is iterable:

for grapheme in g:
    print(grapheme)
# Output:
# ஸ்ரீ
# (space)
# ம
# தி

Why not just list(text)? In Tamil and Sinhala, a single visual character (grapheme) can consist of multiple Unicode code points. For example, ஸ்ரீ is 4 code points but 1 grapheme. Python's list() would split it into 4 separate items, which is linguistically incorrect.

docs.title: 2. Compute Grapheme-Aware Distances
docs.text:
from graphemes_plusplus import levenshtein, hamming

# Levenshtein distance (edit distance)
print(levenshtein("ஸ்ரீ", "ஸ்ரி"))  # 1

# Hamming distance (substitution-only, equal length required)
print(hamming("ஸ்ரீ", "ஸ்ரீ"))     # 0

docs.title: 3. Decompose and Compose
docs.text:
Break graphemes into phonetic components and reconstruct them:

from graphemes_plusplus import decompose, compose

# Decompose into consonant + vowel components
decomposed = decompose("கா")
print(decomposed)  # க் + ஆ components

# Compose back
original = compose(decomposed)
print(original)    # கா

docs.title: 4. Evaluate with Metrics
docs.text:
Use grapheme-aware chrF and CER for NLP evaluation:

from graphemes_plusplus.metric import GraphemeCHRF, CER

# chrF score
chrf = GraphemeCHRF()
score = chrf.corpus_score(
    ["வணக்கம் உலகம்"],
    [["வணக்கம் உலகம்"]]
)
print(score)  # 100.0

# Character Error Rate
cer = CER("predicted text", "reference text")
print(cer)

Next Steps - Explore the full API Reference for detailed documentation - Read the Tamil or Sinhala specific guides - Learn about Evaluation Metrics for NLP tasks

docs.title: Evaluation Metrics
docs.text: A guide to using graphemes++ evaluation metrics for NLP tasks involving Tamil and Sinhala text, such as machine translation, OCR, and speech recognition.

docs.title: Why Grapheme-Level Evaluation?
docs.text:
Standard NLP metrics like chrF and CER operate on Unicode characters. For Indic scripts like Tamil and Sinhala, this leads to inflated or misleading scores because:

  1. A single visual character may be 2–4 Unicode code points
  2. ZWJ sequences are split artificially
  3. Conjuncts are counted as multiple "characters"

graphemes++ solves this by operating at the grapheme cluster level.

docs.title: chrF (Character F-score)
docs.text:
chrF measures n-gram overlap between hypothesis and reference at the character level. GraphemeCHRF does this at the grapheme level.

from graphemes_plusplus.metric import GraphemeCHRF

chrf = GraphemeCHRF()

# Corpus-level scoring
score = chrf.corpus_score(
    ["வணக்கம் உலகம்"],           # hypotheses
    [["வணக்கம் உலகம்"]]          # references
)
print(f"chrF: {score.score:.2f}")  # 100.00

docs.title: chrF++ (with word n-grams)
docs.text:
chrF++ extends chrF by including word-level n-grams, which captures word order information:

chrf_pp = GraphemeCHRF(word_order=2)

# Word order differences are penalized
ref = ["இன்று வானிலை மிகவும் அழகாக இருக்கிறது"]
hyp = ["இருக்கிறது அழகாக மிகவும் வானிலை இன்று"]

score_chrf = GraphemeCHRF().corpus_score(hyp, [ref])
score_chrfpp = chrf_pp.corpus_score(hyp, [ref])

print(f"chrF:  {score_chrf.score:.2f}")   # Grapheme overlap only
print(f"chrF++: {score_chrfpp.score:.2f}") # + word order penalty

docs.title: Multi-Reference Evaluation
docs.text:
GraphemeCHRF supports multiple references (takes the best match):

chrf = GraphemeCHRF()
score = chrf.corpus_score(
    ["வணக்கம்"],
    [["வணக்கம்", "நமஸ்காரம்"]]  # two valid references
)

docs.title: CER (Character Error Rate)
docs.text:
CER measures the grapheme-level edit distance normalized by reference length:

from graphemes_plusplus.metric import CER

# Perfect match
print(CER("வணக்கம்", "வணக்கம்"))  # 0.0

# Complete mismatch
print(CER("", "வணக்கம்"))         # 1.0

# Partial match
cer = CER("வணக்கம", "வணக்கம்")
print(f"CER: {cer:.4f}")

docs.title: CER Formula
docs.text: \[ \text{CER} = \frac{\text{Levenshtein}(\text{hypothesis}, \text{reference})}{|\text{reference graphemes}|} \]

docs.title: Choosing the Right Metric
docs.text: Metric Best For Pros Cons chrF Translation quality No tokenization needed, correlates well with human judgment Ignores word order chrF++ Translation quality Captures word order via word n-grams Slightly more complex N-gram F-score Short sequence similarity Simple precision/recall trade-off Fixed n-gram size CER OCR, ASR Simple, intuitive interpretation Doesn't capture reordering Levenshtein String similarity Raw edit distance Not normalized Hamming Fixed-length comparison Fast Requires equal length BPC Generative models Entropy-style evaluation Hardcoded probabilities

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text:
graph TD
    A["Raw Predictions"] --> B["Graphemizer"]
    C["Ground Truth"] --> D["Graphemizer"]
    B --> E["Grapheme Lists"]
    D --> F["Grapheme Lists"]
    E --> G{"Choose Metric"}
    F --> G
    G --> H["GraphemeCHRF"]
    G --> I["CER / N-gram F-score"]
    G --> J["Levenshtein / Hamming"]
    G --> K["BPC"]

    style A fill:#7c4dff,color:#fff
    style C fill:#7c4dff,color:#fff
    style H fill:#00bfa5,color:#fff
    style I fill:#00bfa5,color:#fff
    style J fill:#00bfa5,color:#fff

For machine translation Use chrF++ (word_order=2) for the best correlation with human judgment on Tamil and Sinhala translation tasks.

For OCR and ASR Use CER for character-level accuracy measurement. It gives a single number between 0 (perfect) and potentially > 1 (very poor).

docs.title: Sinhala Scripts
docs.text: A practical guide to using graphemes++ with Sinhala (සිංහල) text.

docs.title: Why Grapheme-Aware Processing Matters for Sinhala
docs.text:
Sinhala uses Zero Width Joiner (ZWJ) characters to form conjunct consonants. These invisible characters connect multiple consonants into a single visual glyph:

ක්‍රි 1 grapheme · Multiple Unicode code points (with ZWJ)

docs.title: Basic Examples
docs.text:
from graphemes_plusplus import Graphemizer

# Simple Sinhala text
g = Graphemizer("සිංහල")
print(g.graphemes)
# ['සිං', 'හ', 'ල']

# ZWJ conjuncts
g = Graphemizer("ක්‍රිකට්")
print(g.graphemes)
# ['ක්‍රි', 'ක', 'ට්']

docs.title: ZWJ Handling
docs.text:
The standard grapheme library may split Sinhala ZWJ conjuncts incorrectly. graphemes++ detects ZWJ (U+200D) sequences and merges them:

# ZWJ conjuncts are kept as single graphemes
g = Graphemizer("ක්‍රීඩා")
print(g.graphemes)
# ['ක්‍රී', 'ඩා']   correctly merged

Zero Width Joiner (ZWJ) The ZWJ character (U+200D) is invisible but linguistically significant in Sinhala. It tells the rendering engine to form a conjunct ligature. graphemes++ respects this and keeps ZWJ-connected characters together.

docs.title: Sinhala Decomposition
docs.text:
Decompose Sinhala graphemes into consonant base + vowel:

from graphemes_plusplus import decompose, compose

# Decompose
print(decompose("ක"))    # ක් + අ
print(decompose("කා"))   # ක් + ආ
print(decompose("කැ"))   # ක් + ඇ

# Compose back
print(compose(decompose("කා")))  # කා

docs.title: Why Grapheme-Aware Processing Matters for Tamil
docs.text:
Tamil has a complex writing system where a single visual character can consist of multiple Unicode code points:

ஸ்ரீ 1 grapheme · 4 Unicode code points

Representation Count Result len("ஸ்ரீ") 4 Unicode code points len(list("ஸ்ரீ")) 4 Individual characters len(Graphemizer("ஸ்ரீ")) 1 ✅ Correct grapheme count

docs.title: Basic Examples
docs.text:
from graphemes_plusplus import Graphemizer

# Simple word
g = Graphemizer("வணக்கம்")
print(g.graphemes)
# ['வ', 'ண', 'க்', 'க', 'ம்']

# Complex conjunct: க்ஷ
g = Graphemizer("அக்ஷரம்")
print(g.graphemes)
# ['அ', 'க்ஷ', 'ர', 'ம்']

# Sri marker: ஸ்ரீ
g = Graphemizer("ஸ்ரீமான்")
print(g.graphemes)
# ['ஸ்ரீ', 'மா', 'ன்']

docs.title: Tamil Decomposition
docs.text:
Decompose Tamil graphemes into their phonetic components (mei + uyir):

from graphemes_plusplus import decompose, compose

# Decompose: உயிர்மெய் → மெய் + உயிர்

print(decompose("தி"))   # த் + இ
print(decompose("பூ"))   # ப் + ஊ

# Compose back
print(compose(decompose("கா")))  # கா

docs.title: Tamil Normalization
docs.text:
The Normalizer automatically fixes common Tamil encoding issues:

from graphemes_plusplus.utils import Normalizer

n = Normalizer()

# Fix reversed vowel orders
n.normalize("ாெ")  # → ொ
n.normalize("ாே")  # → ோ

# Fix incorrect sequences
n.normalize("ா்")  # → ர்
n.normalize("ாி")  # → ரி

Normalization is automatic When you use Graphemizer, normalization is applied automatically. These examples show the Normalizer for educational purposes.
